Yes, securities lending is a different situation from simply holding fully paid shares in a normal brokerage account.

If you enroll in Fidelity’s Fully Paid Lending Program, Fidelity becomes your counterparty and may relend those shares to third parties. And while the shares are on loan, they are not covered by SIPC. 

But if the hedge fund blows up, that doesn't automatically mean you lose your shares. Fidelity still owes them back to you, and it provides collateral held at a third-party custodial bank, with the collateral marked to market daily and maintained at least equal to the value of the loaned securities. 

So the real risk to you would be if Fidelity itself failed to return the shares, and the collateral somehow proved insufficient.

So yes, there’s legitimate extra risk created by voluntarily lending your shares, but it’s different from the ordinary custody situation I was explaining in the video.

You’re right that the FDIC doesn’t keep enough cash sitting around to reimburse every insured bank deposit in America simultaneously — but that isn’t how deposit insurance is designed to work.

The FDIC’s insurance fund is financed by the banks themselves and backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, and the FDIC has authority to borrow from the Treasury if necessary. Since federal deposit insurance began in 1934, no depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured deposits.

More importantly, though, FDIC isn’t really the point of this video. Stocks and ETFs held at Fidelity or Vanguard aren’t bank deposits. They’re customer securities that are supposed to be kept separate from the brokerage’s own corporate assets.

Lehman Brothers actually failed in 2008, and its customers’ brokerage assets were transferred to other firms.

If the U.S. government itself became unable to honor FDIC insurance and the entire custody system broke down, then yes — we’d be talking about a much larger systemic collapse. But that’s very different from Fidelity, Vanguard or another large financial company going bankrupt.

Strictly speaking, DTC is the central securities depository; DTCC is its parent. If DTC itself failed, you could absolutely see major disruption to trading and settlement. But that still wouldn’t mean DTC suddenly “owns” everyone’s stocks.

Securities registered through DTC’s nominee, Cede & Co., don’t lose their beneficial ownership simply because they’re held in that system. DTC keeps records of broker positions, while the brokers keep the customer-level records showing what belongs to you.

DTC is also designated a systemically important financial-market utility and is required to maintain recovery and orderly wind-down plans specifically for a scenario where it can no longer operate normally.

If DTC itself failed, I’d expect a much messier and more systemic problem than Fidelity failing — think potentially frozen settlement and delayed access while the system works through recovery. But DTC failing still wouldn’t automatically mean everyone’s shares disappear.

At that point, though, we’re getting pretty close to asking what happens if the entire infrastructure of the U.S. securities market itself breaks.

I’m familiar with the argument in The Great Taking, but MF Global does not show that investors holding securities in street name were “legally wiped out.”

In street-name registration, you are still the beneficial owner. SEC rules require brokers to maintain possession or control of fully paid customer securities, and you do not need a physical certificate to have legally recognized ownership rights. 

MF Global was a serious case of customer assets being improperly used. The recovery was long and messy, but securities and commodity-futures customers ultimately received 100% of their allowed customer claims.

Physical stock certificates are no longer the norm because book-entry ownership makes modern trading and settlement far more practical. The system isn’t risk-free—MF Global proves that misconduct can cause real disruption—but “no certificate means you don’t own the shares and can legally be wiped out” is not an accurate description of how it works.

ETFs also have another layer of protection: the fund manager doesn’t simply hold all the underlying assets itself. Registered ETFs are subject to custody requirements, and the fund’s assets are held through custodians and subject to independent reporting/audit requirements.

Madoff was particularly dangerous because he effectively collapsed investment management AND custody into the same operation, removing much of that independent verification.

What about Rehypothecation?

Great question. Rehypothecation is one of the important wrinkles in the way customer securities are protected.

If your shares are fully paid in a regular cash account, the broker generally has to keep them in its possession or control and can’t simply pledge them for its own borrowing. But if you’re borrowing on margin, some of the securities supporting that margin loan can be rehypothecated, subject to regulatory limits.

There’s also voluntary securities lending. Fidelity’s Fully Paid Lending Program, for instance, allows Fidelity to borrow your shares; while they’re on loan, they’re not covered by SIPC (although Fidelity provides collateral worth at least 100% of the loan value held at a third-party custodian).

So yes, rehypothecation adds another layer of counterparty risk, but that doesn’t mean that all customer securities at Fidelity are routinely available for Fidelity to pledge.

Yes, securities lending is a different situation from simply holding fully paid shares in a normal brokerage account.

If you enroll in Fidelity’s Fully Paid Lending Program, Fidelity becomes your counterparty and may relend those shares to third parties. And while the shares are on loan, they are not covered by SIPC. 

But if the hedge fund blows up, that doesn't automatically mean you lose your shares. Fidelity still owes them back to you, and it provides collateral held at a third-party custodial bank, with the collateral marked to market daily and maintained at least equal to the value of the loaned securities. 

So the real risk to you would be if Fidelity itself failed to return the shares, and the collateral somehow proved insufficient.

So yes, there’s legitimate extra risk created by voluntarily lending your shares, but it’s different from the ordinary custody situation I was explaining in the video.

The phrase “up to $250,000” is an absolute dollar ceiling per depositor, not a sliding percentage. If you have $150,000 in an insured account, you are covered for 100% of that $150,000, dollar-for-dollar, backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government—not a pro-rata cut based on the size of the insurance reserve. No depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured funds since FDIC insurance began in 1934.

On cash sweeps: qualifying brokerage sweeps into FDIC-insured partner banks can receive pass-through deposit insurance up to the applicable limits. Sweeps into money-market funds are securities rather than FDIC-insured deposits. And insured bank deposits are not supposed to absorb losses in a bank resolution. But shareholders and certain unsecured creditors can take losses.

@jeffferguson4632 Good point. Legally, SVB did not eliminate the $250,000 FDIC limit. Regulators used the “systemic risk exception,” which is extraordinary authority that allowed them to protect uninsured depositors because they believed losses could trigger broader bank runs. The statutory insurance limit itself never changed. 

So depositors above $250,000 at the next failed bank would not automatically have a legal right to the same treatment. Another systemic-risk determination would have to be made.

But, I do think SVB created an expectation problem. If uninsured depositors at one large bank are made whole because regulators fear contagion, depositors at the next large bank may reasonably expect the same, and depositors at a smaller bank could understandably ask why they were treated differently. In fact, that moral-hazard/fairness issue was one of the concerns raised after SVB.

So I wouldn’t call the $250,000 limit “gone,” but SVB definitely blurred the line between what is formally insured and what the government might choose to protect in a systemic crisis.

I’m familiar with the argument in The Great Taking, but MF Global does not show that investors holding securities in street name were “legally wiped out.”

In street-name registration, you are still the beneficial owner. SEC rules require brokers to maintain possession or control of fully paid customer securities, and you do not need a physical certificate to have legally recognized ownership rights. 

MF Global was a serious case of customer assets being improperly used. The recovery was long and messy, but securities and commodity-futures customers ultimately received 100% of their allowed customer claims.

Physical stock certificates are no longer the norm because book-entry ownership makes modern trading and settlement far more practical. The system isn’t risk-free—MF Global proves that misconduct can cause real disruption—but “no certificate means you don’t own the shares and can legally be wiped out” is not an accurate description of how it works.
